subject: Anthropology
title: Semantics and Pragmatics
description: A quick, practical guide to Semantics and Pragmatics.

hook.text: Can you pass the salt? is not really a question about your ability. Context turns a question into a request.

buildup.text: Semantics studies literal word meaning. Pragmatics studies how context shapes what speakers actually communicate.

discovery.text: The same sentence means different things in different situations. Meaning lives in context, not just in words.

twist.text: Sarcasm, irony, and hints all depend on pragmatics. You say one thing and mean the opposite — and everyone knows.

climax.text: Language is never just literal. Humans constantly read between the lines using shared cultural knowledge.

punchline.text: What you mean is rarely what you say.

quiz.question: What does pragmatics study?
options: How context shapes the meaning of language in use

details.summary: Semantics studies literal meaning while pragmatics studies meaning in context. A sentence's pragmatic meaning often differs from its semantic content — saying 'it's cold in here' may literally describe temperature but pragmatically request closing a window.
details.whyItMatters: Pragmatic meaning drives actual communication far more than literal semantics. Understanding the gap between what is said and what is meant reveals how language functions as a social tool, not just an information transfer system.
takeaways: Semantics studies the literal meaning of words and sentences
Pragmatics studies how context shapes intended meaning
Most real communication relies on pragmatic inference, not literal meaning

faq.question: What is a speech act?
faq.answer: A speech act is an utterance that performs an action — promising, warning, requesting, apologizing. Saying 'I promise to be there' does not describe a promise; it creates one. Speech act theory shows that language does things in the world, not just describes it.

faq.question: How do people understand indirect speech?
faq.answer: Listeners use context, shared knowledge, tone, and social conventions to infer intended meaning beyond literal words. When a dinner host asks 'Can you pass the salt?' no one interprets it as a question about physical ability. Pragmatic competence is learned culturally.
